workingPapers.title: What Does One More AI Agent Contribute? A Microeconomic Review of Delegation, Search, and Verification
workingPapers.abstract: What does a project gain when one more person sends an AI agent to work on it? We review the microeconomics of delegation, innovation contests, public goods, information, and market design through recent cases in mathematics, physics, biomedical research, software, and exchange. An extra attempt at an open problem can expand the set of solutions, improve an input that others use, or supply a second opinion. Each activity has a different return to entry. The contest literature emphasizes the diversity of attempts, the economics of cumulative innovation emphasizes downstream reuse, and information economics asks what a second report reveals conditional on the first. Which return a project can capture also depends on who supplies review and what the acceptance rule measures. Comparing a public proof desk with evidence extraction for rare diseases illustrates why duplicate work can waste resources in one assignment and be the purpose of another. We propose ways to distinguish these mechanisms using assignment, audit, and reuse records.

workingPapers.title: AI Agent Unemployment
workingPapers.abstract: Why would a subscriber leave an AI agent idle when another useful task is ready? Saving the last unit of a weekly allowance preserves the ability to handle urgent work. We study a subscriber who can also authorize a routine task to start if urgent work fails to arrive. The subscribers most willing to pay for this option are those initially indifferent between running the routine task and saving the unit. Among adopters, the probability that the unit expires falls for those who previously held it in reserve and rises for those who previously ran the routine task. Both groups gain in expected value. Two populations with the same initial unused share can therefore respond to the same offer in opposite directions. The amount of unused quota alone does not, in general, tell us how much subscribers gain from delegation.

workingPapers.title: Portable Checkpoints Can Reduce Completion
workingPapers.abstract: We study a procurement contract in which the incumbent privately learns its opportunity cost of completion after delivering a verifiable intermediate output that a replacement can use. Greater replacement availability raises expected surplus but can lower the probability of project completion: under the optimal contract, the completion bonus falls, inducing some incumbents to exit before they know whether a replacement is available. If availability is observed before exit and the bonus can depend on it, greater replacement availability never lowers the completion probability and raises it if and only if some incumbents would exit even when no replacement is available.

notes.title: What could we do with spare AI time?
notes.summary: A market could put spare AI usage to work. The first model asks how the prospect of a backup changes the incentive to finish a task.
